claims.claim: egg production from the Rose et al. 1999 model, via Rose et al. 2001
claims.conditions: simulated (individual-based model of Oneida Lake), means over the last 35 of 50 years; 0.80, 1.11 and 1.35 million eggs/ha for decreased, baseline and increased yellow perch egg mortality. The table is 'from Rose et al. 1999'
claims.note: Same values as Rose et al. 1999 Table 9; cite the 1999 original (read in full in this batch). See Rose_etal_1999.json for the arithmetic caveat on the 0.04–0.09 %.

claims.claim: halving or raising egg mortality changed first feeders 4.4-fold but age-2 recruits by only about 8 % (205, 210 and 221 per hectare), and the share mature at age 4 rose from 24 % to 54 % (Rose et al. 1999, via Rose et al. 2001)
claims.location: p. 308 (PDF p. 16), Table 1 and text; p. 309 (PDF p. 17)
claims.quote: Lower number of ﬁrst feeders No. ha–1 178 325 85 036 40 894
claims.conditions: model predictions. Baseline egg mortality 0.11/d, raised to 0.15/d and lowered to 0.06/d. Recruitment = abundance at age 2; 'percentage mature (age-4)' 24, 41, 54
claims.note: 178,325/40,894 = 4.36; (221 − 205)/205 = 7.8 %. The 2001 text gives the chain: faster growth of young perch, faster adult growth, younger maturation. With adult numbers 'near or slightly above baseline' (103–112/ha), the extra spawners and fecundity raise egg production enough to compensate.

claims.claim: Real lakes: survival 18 mm → age 2 doubles each time density halves, so recruits stay within ~8 % across a fourfold range (Oneida perch: 0.41, 0.85, 1.56 %, Rose et al. 2001)
claims.source_value: the numbers hold (18-mm abundance 60,594 / 30,329 / 15,325 per ha, a 3.95-fold range; survival 18 mm → recruitment 0.41 / 0.85 / 1.56 %; recruitment 205 / 210 / 221 per ha), but they are SIMULATED, an individual-based model's 35-year means, not observations in a real lake
claims.quote: Increased 18 mm to recruitment survival Percentage 0.41 0.85 1.56
claims.conditions: Oneida Lake yellow perch–walleye IBM (Rose et al. 1999), egg mortality varied 0.06 / 0.11 / 0.15 per day
claims.note: Change 'Real lakes:' to 'In the Oneida Lake IBM (Rose et al. 1999, Table 9; via Rose et al. 2001, Table 1):'. 'Doubles each time density halves' holds roughly (0.85/0.41 = 2.07; 1.56/0.85 = 1.84). In the model the survival rise comes mainly from lighter walleye predation as walleye declined (20.2 → 16.1 adults/ha), not only from the perch's own density.

notes: Rose et al. 2001 is a review. Its Oneida example is a secondary presentation of Rose et al. 1999 (both read). Point the paper's Oneida model numbers at the 1999 original, and keep 2001 for the review's general statements.
